newsitem.title: USA: CBOT soybeans end mostly down, Aug soars on supply.
newsitem.headline: CBOT soybeans end mostly down, Aug soars on supply.

text.p: CBOT August soybeans surged higher on Friday, gaining more than 50 cents this week on thin nearby supplies, while new crop months ended barely changed amid mixed signals from world weather forecasts, traders said.
"The shorts are on the run and it's going to be extremely volatile," an analyst said, referring to the August. "We still have quite a bit of open interest left ahead of expiry."

Pit sources pointed to firm cash basis levels in the country and at the U.S. Gulf as well as National Oilseed Processors Association crush data which suggested demand remained strong for dwindling old crop supplies.
NOPA on Friday said there were 24.34 million bushels of soybeans crushed in the week of August 13, above trade expectation. NOPA's monthly crush figure for July also exceeded trade expectations.
The August contract expires on Wednesday. CBOT said open interest was at 21.795 million bushels as of Thursday.
Soybeans closed 19-1/2 cents per bushel higher to 1/2 cent lower with August up 19-1/2 cents at $7.91-3/4 per bushel.
Forecasts for rain this week in the U.S. Midwest and the U.S. South were deemed bearish for new crop months but lent even more strength to the August.

"They planted some early-maturing varieties down there and those rains could slow harvest," an oilseed analyst said. "We were counting on some of those beans reaching southeast crushers in the first half of September."
New crop months continued to struggle with the forecasts which led to ideas new crop supplies would grow even larger.
USDA on Tuesday forecast a record crop and trade sources said ideal growing conditions in the next few weeks could add even more bushels.
But new crop months drew strength from weather forecasts for India and China, which led to ideas of potential yield losses there.
Smith Barney meteorologist Jon Davis said monsoonal rains in India had started to diminish in recent days.

"This is a very unusual situation to occur during the middle of August," Davis wrote. "It means one of two things. Either the monsoonal activity is taking a break and it will rebuild later in August or the monsoon is starting to retreat."

Davis also said there were no rains this past week in central China and only spotty showers in northern China. Forecasts called for dry weather for the next few days with the next chance of rain there coming on Sunday or Monday.

There was also speculation about whether El Nino would cause weather-related problems in Brazil and Argentina when they begin planting later this year. El Nino is strongly correlated with both flooding and drought in southern Brazil growing areas, meteorologists said.

On the day, Refco Inc bought two million bushels November and sold 2.5 million, floor sources said. Smith Barney and E.D. and F. Man International each bought 2.5 million November while Term Commodities sold one million.
In spread trade, Goldenberg-Hehmeyer spread two million August/November at $1.68 to $1.73, premium August, traders said.

In options, Refco bought 400 November $5.25 puts at one cent, Farmers Commodities Corp bought 200 November $6.00 puts at 14 cents and sold 600 November $5.50 puts at three cents, and ADM bought 300 September $7.00 calls at 4-1/4.
Volatility in the November was pegged at 19-1/4 percent, down slightly from Thursday's 19-3/4 percent.
Soybean futures volume was estimated by CBOT at 45,000 contracts, compared with Thursday's actual volume of 47,839.
